'''''Mata v. Avianca, Inc.''''' was a [[United States District Court for the Southern District of New York|U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York]] case in which the Court dismissed a [[personal injury]] case against the airline [[Avianca]] and issued a $5,000 fine to the plaintiffs' lawyers who had submitted fake [[precedent]]s generated by [[ChatGPT]] in their [[Brief (law)|legal briefs]].<ref name=":1" />

== Background ==
In February 2022, Roberto Mata filed a personal injury lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against Avianca, alleging that he was injured when a metal serving cart struck his knee during an international flight. The plaintiff's lawyers used ChatGPT to generate a [[Motion (legal)|legal motion]], which contained numerous fake legal cases involving fictitious airlines with fabricated quotations and internal citations.<ref>{{cite news |last=Goswami |first=Rohan |date=May 30, 2023 |title=ChatGPT cited 'bogus' cases for a New York federal court filing. The attorneys involved may face sanctions. |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/05/30/chatgpt-cited-bogus-cases-for-a-new-york-federal-court-filing.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230530161531/https://www.cnbc.com/2023/05/30/chatgpt-cited-bogus-cases-for-a-new-york-federal-court-filing.html |archive-date=May 30, 2023 |access-date=May 30, 2023 |publisher=CNBC}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Neumeister |first=Larry |date=June 8, 2023 |title=Lawyers blame ChatGPT for tricking them into citing bogus case law |url=https://apnews.com/article/artificial-intelligence-chatgpt-courts-e15023d7e6fdf4f099aa122437dbb59b |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231108131752/https://apnews.com/article/artificial-intelligence-chatgpt-courts-e15023d7e6fdf4f099aa122437dbb59b |archive-date=November 8, 2023 |access-date=November 8, 2023 |publisher=Associated Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=June 24, 2023 |title='Use with caution': How ChatGPT landed this US lawyer and his firm in hot water |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-06-24/us-lawyer-uses-chatgpt-to-research-case-with-embarrassing-result/102490068 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231109010855/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-06-24/us-lawyer-uses-chatgpt-to-research-case-with-embarrassing-result/102490068 |archive-date=November 9, 2023 |access-date=November 9, 2023 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref>

Avianca's lawyers notified the Court that they had been "unable to locate" a few legal cases cited in the legal motion. The Court could not locate the cases either and ordered the plaintiff's lawyers to provide copies of the cited legal cases. Mata's lawyers provided copies of documents purportedly containing all but one of the legal cases, after ChatGPT assured that the cases "indeed exist" and "can be found in reputable legal databases such as [[LexisNexis]] and [[Westlaw]]."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=June 22, 2023 |title=Mata v. Avianca, Inc. |url=https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/6499235932898b72d5cfb1aa |access-date=May 14, 2025 |website=casemine.com}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Maruf |first=Ramishah |date=2023-05-27 |title=Lawyer apologizes for fake court citations from ChatGPT {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/05/27/business/chat-gpt-avianca-mata-lawyers/index.html |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

== Opinion ==
In May 2023, Judge [[P. Kevin Castel]] dismissed the personal injury case against Avianca and ordered the plaintiff's attorneys to pay a $5,000 fine.<ref name=":1" />

Judge Castel noted numerous inconsistencies in the opinion summaries, describing one of the legal analyses as "gibberish."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brodkin |first1=Jon |date=June 23, 2023 |title=Lawyers have real bad day in court after citing fake cases made up by ChatGPT |url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2023/06/lawyers-have-real-bad-day-in-court-after-citing-fake-cases-made-up-by-chatgpt/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240126071502/https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2023/06/lawyers-have-real-bad-day-in-court-after-citing-fake-cases-made-up-by-chatgpt/ |archive-date=January 26, 2024 |access-date=February 18, 2024 |work=Ars Technica |language=en-us}}</ref> Judge Castel held that Mata's lawyers had acted with "subjective bad faith" sufficient for sanctions under [[Federal Rules of Civil Procedure|Federal Rule of Civil Procedure]] Rule 11.<ref name=":1" />  

== Impact ==
In July 2024, the [[American Bar Association]] issued its first formal ethics opinion on the responsibilities of lawyers using [[Generative artificial intelligence|generative AI]] (GAI). The 15-page opinion outlines how the [[American Bar Association Model Rules of Professional Conduct|Rules of Professional Conduct]] apply to the use of GAI in the practice of law.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ABA issues first ethics guidance on a lawyer’s use of AI tools |url=https://www.americanbar.org/news/abanews/aba-news-archives/2024/07/aba-issues-first-ethics-guidance-ai-tools/ |access-date=2025-05-15 |website=www.americanbar.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Merken |first=Sara |date=July 29, 2024 |title=Lawyers using AI must heed ethics rules, ABA says in first formal guidance |url=https://www.reuters.com/legal/legalindustry/lawyers-using-ai-must-heed-ethics-rules-aba-says-first-formal-guidance-2024-07-29/ |access-date=April 24, 2025 |website=Reuters}}</ref>

Experts caution that lawyers cannot reasonably rely on the accuracy, completeness, or validity of content generated by GAI tools.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Reviewing Generative Artificial Intelligence False Citations |url=https://natlawreview.com/article/new-aba-guidance-generative-artificial-intelligence-use-what-it-means-legal |access-date=2025-05-15 |website=natlawreview.com |language=en}}</ref>

Due to the continued usage of GAI in the practice of law, ''Mata'' has been described as a landmark case by legal professionals,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Charlotin |first1=Damien |title=AI Hallucination Cases |url=https://www.damiencharlotin.com/hallucinations/ |website=damiencharlotin.com |access-date=4 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Curlin |first1=James |title=ChatGPT Didn’t Write This . . . or Did It? The Emergence of Generative AI in the Legal Field and Lessons from Mata v. Avianca |journal=Arkansas Law Review |date=May 2025 |volume=78 |issue=1 |page=130-132 |url=https://scholarworks.uark.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1277&context=alr |access-date=4 June 2025}}</ref> as it is frequently cited by courts in cases where usage of GAI during the course of proceedings leads to the creation and citation of nonexistent caselaw.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gauthier v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. |url=https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/6746a063e8c044126187cfea |website=Casemine |access-date=4 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Benjamin v. Costco Wholesale Corporation |url=https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-ed-new-yor/117206693.html |website=FindLaw |access-date=4 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Johnson v. Dunn |url=https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.alnd.179677/gov.uscourts.alnd.179677.204.0.pdf |website=CourtListener |access-date=29 July 2025}}</ref>
